title: GATE Mathematics Topic Test: Functional Analysis — Set 2
titleEn: GATE Mathematics Topic Test: Functional Analysis — Set 2
titleHi: गेट गणित टॉपिक टेस्ट: फलनिक विश्लेषण — सेट 2

questions.questionTextEn: For which value of $p \in [1, \infty]$ is the norm $\|\cdot\|_p$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ induced by an inner product?
questions.explanationEn: A norm is induced by an inner product iff it satisfies the parallelogram law $\|x+y\|^2 + \|x-y\|^2 = 2(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2)$. Taking $x = (1, 0)$ and $y = (0, 1)$, we need $2^{2/p} + 2^{2/p} = 2(1 + 1) = 4$, i.e., $2^{2/p} = 2$, which holds if and only if $p = 2$.

questions.questionTextEn: Which one of the following Banach spaces is NOT separable?
questions.explanationEn: The subset $S = \{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \subset \ell^\infty$ of all binary sequences is uncountable, and for any two distinct $x, y \in S$, $\|x - y\|_\infty = 1$. Hence open balls of radius $1/2$ centered at points of $S$ are pairwise disjoint, so no countable dense subset can exist in $\ell^\infty$. In contrast, $\ell^1$, $\ell^2$, and $(C[0,1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ are all separable.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be a normed linear space and $x_0 \in X$ be a nonzero vector. By the Hahn-Banach theorem, there exists a bounded linear functional $f \in X^*$ such that:
optionsEn: $f$ is unique for every normed linear space $X$
questions.explanationEn: Define $g(\alpha x_0) = \alpha \|x_0\|$ on the $1$-dimensional subspace $M = \operatorname{span}\{x_0\}$. Then $g \in M^*$ with $\|g\| = 1$ and $g(x_0) = \|x_0\|$. By the Hahn-Banach theorem, $g$ extends to $f \in X^*$ with $\|f\| = \|g\| = 1$ and $f(x_0) = \|x_0\|$. Uniqueness fails in general (e.g., in $(\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_1)$).

questions.questionTextEn: Which one of the following Banach spaces is REFLEXIVE?
questions.explanationEn: For $1 < p < \infty$, $(\ell^p)^* \cong \ell^q$ and $(\ell^p)^{**} \cong (\ell^q)^* \cong \ell^p$ via the canonical embedding, where $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1$. Thus $\ell^3$ is reflexive. In contrast, $c_0$, $\ell^1$, and $\ell^\infty$ are all non-reflexive (e.g., $(c_0)^{**} \cong \ell^\infty \neq c_0$).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{C}$. Which of the following statements is/are ALWAYS true?
optionsEn: Any two norms on $X$ are equivalent.
Every linear operator $T: X \to Y$ into any normed linear space $Y$ is bounded.
Every linear subspace of $X$ is closed.
questions.explanationEn: All four are fundamental properties of finite-dimensional normed spaces: all norms are equivalent (A), every linear map out of $X$ is continuous (B), $X$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^n$ and hence complete under any norm (C), and every subspace is finite-dimensional, hence complete, hence closed (D).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X, Y, Z$ be Banach spaces, $T \in \mathcal{B}(X, Y)$ be a compact operator, and $S \in \mathcal{B}(Y, Z)$ be a bounded operator. Which of the following statements is/are ALWAYS true?
optionsEn: $ST: X \to Z$ is a compact operator.
Every finite-rank bounded linear operator is compact.
If $X = Y$ is infinite-dimensional, then $T$ cannot have a bounded inverse.
The range $R(T)$ is always closed in $Y$.
questions.explanationEn: (A) is true: compact operators form a two-sided ideal in $\mathcal{B}$. (B) is true by Bolzano-Weierstrass in finite-dimensional subspaces. (C) is true: if $T^{-1}$ were bounded, then $I = T^{-1}T$ would be compact on an infinite-dimensional space, impossible. (D) is false: a compact operator has closed range iff it has finite rank (e.g., $T(x_n) = (x_n/n)$ on $\ell^2$ has dense, non-closed range).

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following dual-space identifications (up to isometric isomorphism) is/are CORRECT?
questions.explanationEn: (A), (C), and (D) are standard Riesz representation dualities (for $p=3$, the conjugate exponent is $q = \frac{3}{3-1} = \frac{3}{2}$). (B) is false because $\ell^1$ is separable whereas $(\ell^\infty)^*$ is non-separable (in fact $\ell^1$ embeds strictly into $(\ell^\infty)^*$).

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the linear functional $h: (\mathbb{R}^3, \|\cdot\|_\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $h(x_1, x_2, x_3) = 2x_1 - 5x_2 + 3x_3$. The operator norm $\|h\|$ is ______.
questions.explanationEn: The dual norm of $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is $\|\cdot\|_1$. Hence $\|h\| = |2| + |-5| + |3| = 10$, attained at $x = (1, -1, 1)$.

questions.questionTextEn: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the standard Euclidean inner product, let $M = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 0, 1)\}$. The square of the shortest distance from the vector $x = (1, 2, 3)$ to $M$ is ______.
questions.explanationEn: Let $u = (1, 0, 1)$. The orthogonal projection of $x = (1, 2, 3)$ onto $M$ is $P_M x = \frac{\langle x, u \rangle}{\|u\|^2} u = \frac{1 + 0 + 3}{1 + 0 + 1}(1, 0, 1) = (2, 0, 2)$. The residual is $x - P_M x = (-1, 2, 1)$, so the squared distance is $\|x - P_M x\|^2 = (-1)^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 6$.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the compact self-adjoint integral operator $T: L^2[0, 1] \to L^2[0, 1]$ defined by $(Tf)(t) = \int_0^1 6ts\,f(s)\,ds$. The largest eigenvalue of $T$ is ______.
questions.explanationEn: The range of $T$ is the $1$-dimensional subspace $\operatorname{span}\{t\}$, so any nonzero eigenfunction must be a scalar multiple of $f(t) = t$. Applying $T$ to $f(s) = s$ gives $(Tf)(t) = 6t \int_0^1 s^2\,ds = 6t \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 2t$. Hence the unique nonzero (and largest) eigenvalue is $\lambda = 2$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be a normed linear space. Which one of the following statements about reflexivity is TRUE?
optionsEn: Every closed subspace of a reflexive Banach space is reflexive.
Every separable Banach space is reflexive.
Every Banach space with a separable dual is reflexive.
A Banach space $X$ is reflexive if and only if $X$ is isometrically isomorphic to $X^*$.
questions.explanationEn: (A) is a standard theorem (a closed subspace of a reflexive Banach space is reflexive). (B) fails for $\ell^1$ and $c_0$. (C) fails for $c_0$ (whose dual $\ell^1$ is separable). (D) is false: reflexivity requires the CANONICAL embedding $J: X \to X^{**}$ to be surjective (not $X \cong X^*$; e.g., $\ell^3$ is reflexive yet $\ell^3 \not\cong \ell^{3/2}$).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and $T \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ be a compact operator. Which one of the following operators is ALWAYS Fredholm / invertible-up-to-finite-rank, and in particular has CLOSED range?
questions.explanationEn: By the Riesz-Schauder (Fredholm alternative) theory for compact operators, for any nonzero scalar $\lambda \neq 0$ (in particular $\lambda = 1$), the operator $\lambda I - T$ always has closed range, finite-dimensional kernel, and finite-codimensional range. In contrast, $T$, $T^2$, and $T^*T$ are compact and have non-closed range whenever they have infinite rank.

questions.questionTextEn: In a complex Hilbert space $H$, let $T \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ satisfy $\langle Tx, x \rangle = 0$ for all $x \in H$. Then:
optionsEn: $T$ must be a nonzero unitary operator.
$T$ can be nonzero if $T$ is skew-adjoint ($T^* = -T$).
questions.explanationEn: Over $\mathbb{C}$, the polarization identity for the sesquilinear form $\langle Tx, y \rangle$ expresses $\langle Tx, y \rangle = \frac{1}{4}\big(\langle T(x+y), x+y \rangle - \langle T(x-y), x-y \rangle + i\langle T(x+iy), x+iy \rangle - i\langle T(x-iy), x-iy \rangle\big)$. Since every term on the right vanishes, $\langle Tx, y \rangle = 0$ for all $x, y \in H$, forcing $T = 0$. (Note: over $\mathbb{R}$, a $90^\circ$ rotation on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a nonzero counterexample.)

questions.questionTextEn: Let $H$ be the real Hilbert space $L^2[0, 1]$ and define $f \in H^*$ by $f(g) = \int_0^{1/2} g(t)\,dt - \int_{1/2}^1 g(t)\,dt$. What is the unique Riesz representer $h \in L^2[0, 1]$ such that $f(g) = \langle g, h \rangle$ for all $g \in L^2[0, 1]$, and what is $\|f\|$?
questions.explanationEn: We can write $f(g) = \int_0^1 g(t) h(t)\,dt$ with $h(t) = 1$ on $[0, 1/2]$ and $h(t) = -1$ on $(1/2, 1]$, i.e., $h = \chi_{[0, 1/2]} - \chi_{(1/2, 1]} \in L^2[0, 1]$. By Riesz Representation, $\|f\| = \|h\|_2 = \left(\int_0^1 |h(t)|^2\,dt\right)^{1/2} = \left(\int_0^1 1\,dt\right)^{1/2} = 1$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be a Banach space and $M$ be a closed subspace of $X$. Equip the quotient space $X/M$ with the quotient norm $\|x + M\| = \inf_{m \in M} \|x - m\|$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
optionsEn: The canonical quotient map $\pi: X \to X/M$ is a bounded linear operator with $\|\pi\| \le 1$.
The quotient map $\pi: X \to X/M$ is an open map.
If $X$ is separable, then $X/M$ is separable.
questions.explanationEn: All four are standard theorems: the quotient of a Banach space by a closed subspace is complete (A); $\|\pi(x)\| = \inf_{m \in M} \|x - m\| \le \|x\|$ gives $\|\pi\| \le 1$ (B); $\pi$ is surjective and bounded between Banach spaces, hence open by the Open Mapping Theorem (C); and the continuous image $\pi(D)$ of a countable dense subset $D \subset X$ is countable and dense in $X/M$ (D).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be a normed linear space and $Y$ be a linear subspace of $X$. Which of the following statements is/are ALWAYS true?
optionsEn: $Y$ is dense in $X$ if and only if every $f \in X^*$ that vanishes on $Y$ is identically zero on $X$.
If $x_0 \in X \setminus \overline{Y}$, then there exists $f \in X^*$ such that $f|_Y = 0$ and $f(x_0) = 1$.
If $X$ is infinite-dimensional, then $X^*$ is also infinite-dimensional.
Every linear functional on $Y$ (not necessarily bounded) extends to a bounded linear functional on $X$.
questions.explanationEn: (A) and (B) are direct corollaries of the Hahn-Banach separation theorem. (C) holds because by Hahn-Banach, linearly independent vectors $x_1, \dots, x_n$ admit dual functionals $f_1, \dots, f_n \in X^*$ with $f_i(x_j) = \delta_{ij}$, which are linearly independent for arbitrary $n$. (D) is false: an unbounded functional on $Y$ cannot have a bounded extension to $X$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $B: H \times H \to \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded sesquilinear form (linear in the first argument, conjugate-linear in the second, with $|B(x, y)| \le M\|x\|\|y\|$ for all $x, y \in H$). Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
optionsEn: There exists a unique bounded linear operator $T \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ such that $B(x, y) = \langle Tx, y \rangle$ for all $x, y \in H$.
$T$ is self-adjoint if and only if $B(x, y) = \overline{B(y, x)}$ for all $x, y \in H$.
If $B(x, x) \ge c\|x\|^2$ for some $c > 0$ and all $x \in H$, then $T$ is invertible in $\mathcal{B}(H)$ (Lax-Milgram).
questions.explanationEn: (A) and (B) follow directly from applying the Riesz Representation Theorem to $y \mapsto \overline{B(x, y)}$. (C) holds since $\langle Tx, y \rangle = \langle x, Ty \rangle \iff B(x, y) = \overline{\langle Ty, x \rangle} = \overline{B(y, x)}$. (D) is the Lax-Milgram Theorem: coercivity implies $T$ is bounded below (injective with closed range) and has dense range, hence bijective with bounded inverse.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the compact self-adjoint Hilbert-Schmidt operator $T: L^2[0, 1] \to L^2[0, 1]$ defined by $(Tf)(t) = \int_0^1 6(t + s - 1) f(s)\,ds$. If $\{\lambda_n\}$ denotes the sequence of eigenvalues of $T$ counted with multiplicity, then the value of $\sum_n \lambda_n^2$ is ______.
questions.explanationEn: For a compact self-adjoint Hilbert-Schmidt operator with kernel $K(t, s) \in L^2([0, 1]^2)$, $\sum_n \lambda_n^2 = \|T\|_{\text{HS}}^2 = \int_0^1 \int_0^1 |K(t, s)|^2\,ds\,dt$. Here $\int_0^1 \int_0^1 36(t + s - 1)^2\,ds\,dt = 36 \int_0^1 \left[\frac{(t+s-1)^3}{3}\right]_{s=0}^{s=1} dt = 12 \int_0^1 (t^3 - (t-1)^3)\,dt = 12\left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\right) = 6$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A: (\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_2) \to (\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_2)$ be the linear operator represented in the standard basis by the symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. The operator norm $\|A\|$ is ______.
questions.explanationEn: For a real symmetric matrix, the Euclidean operator norm equals the largest absolute eigenvalue. The characteristic polynomial is $(5 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = (\lambda - 6)(\lambda - 1) = 0$, giving eigenvalues $6$ and $1$. Hence $\|A\| = 6$.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the integral operator $T: (C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty) \to (C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ defined by $(Tf)(t) = \int_0^1 (t^2 + s) f(s)\,ds$. The operator norm $\|T\|$ (rounded off to one decimal place) is ______.
questions.explanationEn: For an integral operator with continuous kernel $K(t, s)$ on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$, $\|T\| = \max_{t \in [0, 1]} \int_0^1 |K(t, s)|\,ds$. Since $t^2 + s \ge 0$ on $[0, 1]^2$, $\int_0^1 (t^2 + s)\,ds = t^2 + \frac{1}{2}$, whose maximum on $[0, 1]$ is $1 + \frac{1}{2} = 1.5$ (attained by $f \equiv 1$ at $t = 1$).
